title: Fuelling in the Tropics: Water, Sodium and Food for Hot-Weather Racing
seo_title: Fuelling in the Tropics: Water, Sodium and Food for Hot Races
meta_description: How much runners sweat, why overdrinking is the bigger danger, the sodium and carbohydrate numbers that matter, and what the region's isotonic drinks, gels and local food actually offer.
dek: In humid heat a runner can lose a litre or two of sweat an hour, and the salt in it varies several-fold from one person to the next. What the sports-medicine evidence says about replacing it, and how to use what is actually on the shelf and at the aid stations here.

sections.heading: How Much You Sweat, and What Is in It
paragraphs: A review of sweat testing in athletes found whole-body sweat rates typically between about 0.5 and 2.0 litres an hour, and sodium concentrations in sweat of roughly 10 to 70 mmol per litre across the whole body [3]. That is a sevenfold spread in salt alone, which is why no single drink suits everyone. Heat acclimatisation helps: as the body adapts, sweat glands reabsorb more sodium and sweat gets less salty [3].

The American College of Sports Medicine's fluid guidance follows from that variability. Its goal for drinking during exercise is to avoid losing more than 2% of body weight to a water deficit, and because sweat rates differ so much, it recommends an individual plan built on weighing yourself before and after training [2]. A runner who weighs 60 kg before an hour-long run in the heat and 59 kg after has sweated roughly a litre more than they drank. The heat consensus statement adds that drinking to thirst may not keep up when sweat rates are high [1], so a heavy sweater on a long run needs a rough plan, not just instinct.

sections.heading: The Opposite Danger: Drinking Too Much
paragraphs: More water is not automatically safer. Exercise-associated hyponatraemia, a dangerous fall in blood sodium, is usually caused by drinking too much plain water or sports drink, according to the Wilderness Medical Society's guidelines as summarised by the American Academy of Family Physicians. The society's advice is to limit drinking to what thirst calls for, and it notes that no fixed drinking volume has been shown to prevent the condition [4].

Salt does not cancel out overdrinking. The same guidance says salty food is reasonable to have on long efforts in the heat, but it will not prevent hyponatraemia if a runner drinks too much [4]. The heat consensus puts the two risks together neatly: minimise the water you lose, but never finish heavier than you started [1]. Weight gain over a long run or race is the warning sign.

sections.heading: Sodium and Carbohydrate: The Numbers That Matter
paragraphs: For exercise lasting more than an hour in the heat, the consensus statement suggests drinks carrying 0.5 to 0.7 grams of sodium per litre and 30 to 60 grams of carbohydrate an hour [1]. Under an hour, water is enough for most runners. Over two hours, which covers every marathon and most half marathons in this region, both numbers matter. Before a long run or race, it suggests about 6 ml of fluid per kilogram of body weight every two to three hours to start properly hydrated, and after it, replacing 100% to 150% of the weight lost [1].

Carbohydrate works best taken early and steadily: start in the first 30 to 45 minutes and keep going at regular intervals rather than waiting for the first sign of fading. Heat blunts appetite, which makes a timer more reliable than hunger. Take gels with water rather than with a sports drink, so you do not stack two sugary doses at once.

Aid stations here are close together. Of the 41 races in our calendar whose records state the spacing, the median was a station every 2 km, and 40 of the 41 had stations 2.5 km apart or closer [14]. That makes it easy to drink little and often, and easy to overdrink. Find out what your race hands out (water only, or an isotonic drink as well) and train with that product.

sections.heading: The Local Shelf: Isotonic Drinks and Gels
paragraphs: The drink at the aid station is often a regional brand. 100PLUS was launched in Malaysia under the F&N group in 1983 [8]. Pocari Sweat, launched by Japan's Otsuka in 1980, is sold in the Philippines, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand among other markets [9]. TCP Group calls Sponsor Thailand's number one sports drink, and in 2024 it launched a separate, less sweet Sponsor Isotonic [10]. Several brands put their names on races in our calendar: Pocari Sweat Run in Bandung and a Pocari Sweat Run Carnival in Thailand, Sponsor Run Bangkok, the Surabaya Isoplus Marathon and the Gatorade BKK Run, alongside 13 legs of the National MILO Marathon in the Philippines [14].

Check the label rather than the marketing. Some isotonic drinks are fairly salty and others are mostly sugar water; compare the sodium per litre with the 0.5 to 0.7 g guide above. Carbonated versions are better saved for after the finish.

Locally made gels are rarer. Thailand's Dever started in 2011, developed by a team of dietitians, food technologists and sports scientists, and sells 40 ml and 100 ml packs; it launched in Malaysia at the Kuala Lumpur marathon expo in 2022 [11]. For daily training, electrolyte tablets and powder sachets are the cheaper route: they turn the water bottle you already carry into a sports drink and let you make it stronger on hotter days. Whatever you use, test it on long runs first.

sections.heading: Coconut Water, Bananas and Other Local Food
paragraphs: Coconut water holds up better than most natural sports-drink claims. In a controlled study, 12 trained men were dehydrated by about 2% of body weight on a treadmill and then rehydrated with coconut water, a sports drink or plain water. All of them rehydrated similarly and performed similarly afterwards, but the men reported more bloating and stomach upset after coconut water [5]. It is better as a post-race drink than a mid-race one.

Its composition varies. The US Department of Agriculture lists 250 mg of potassium, 105 mg of sodium and 3.7 g of carbohydrate per 100 g of coconut water [6], but packaged brands and individual coconuts differ, so read the label if you are counting sodium. It is low in carbohydrate compared with a sports drink, so it does not fuel a race.

Bananas, sold at most finish lines, are a carbohydrate and potassium food, not a salt food: about 23 g of carbohydrate, 358 mg of potassium and 1 mg of sodium per 100 g [7]. Watermelon and other cut fruit add fluid. After a long, sweaty race, pair the fruit with something salty, then eat a proper meal with protein and starch within a couple of hours.

sections.heading: Halal Sports Nutrition
paragraphs: For many runners in Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei, halal status is a deciding factor. Ingredients to check in sports products include gelatin, which is common in chews and some gels, and alcohol-based flavourings. A certification mark is a stronger signal than a line saying the product contains no pork.

Indonesia has made halal certification compulsory for food and drink sold by medium and large businesses since 18 October 2024, with micro and small businesses and imported food and drink given until 17 October 2026 [12]. In Malaysia, JAKIM recognises foreign halal certification bodies to certify products entering the market; in 2024 the religious affairs minister put their number at 88, covering 49 countries [13]. Imported gels can therefore carry a valid halal certificate even if they are not made in the region. Fasting runners can find timing advice for training and racing in Ramadan at runsea.run/articles/running-through-ramadan-guide-for-muslim-runners/.

faqs.question: Is plain water enough on a long, hot run?
faqs.answer: Under about an hour, yes for most runners. Beyond that, the heat consensus statement suggests drinks with 0.5 to 0.7 g of sodium per litre and 30 to 60 g of carbohydrate an hour. Plain water alone, drunk in large amounts over several hours, is the classic route to low blood sodium.

faqs.question: Can drinking too much water on a run be dangerous?
faqs.answer: Yes. Exercise-associated hyponatraemia, a dangerous fall in blood sodium, is usually caused by drinking more water or sports drink than you lose. The Wilderness Medical Society advises drinking to thirst, and salt tablets do not protect a runner who overdrinks. Finishing a long run heavier than you started is the warning sign.

faqs.question: Is coconut water as good as a sports drink?
faqs.answer: For rehydrating after exercise, roughly yes: in a controlled study it rehydrated as well as a sports drink and plain water, though it caused more bloating. It carries little carbohydrate and its sodium varies by brand, so it is a recovery drink rather than race fuel.

faqs.question: How do I know if a gel or drink is halal?
faqs.answer: Look for a certification mark, not just a 'no pork' claim. Indonesia has required halal certification for food and drink from medium and large businesses since October 2024, and Malaysia's JAKIM recognises dozens of foreign certification bodies, so imported products can carry a valid halal certificate.
